mcqs.question: Why is object storage's lack of a built-in schema actually an advantage for a data lake's ingestion process?
options: It means data never needs to be modeled at any point in its lifecycle
It lets data be written the moment it's available, in whatever shape the source produces, without a schema design step blocking ingestion
It makes queries automatically faster than a warehouse's structured tables
It guarantees the data will never need cleaning
mcqs.explanation: The schema-less nature of object storage removes the schema-design step as a blocker to writing data, which is the specific advantage for ingestion speed and flexibility. It doesn't remove the eventual need to model data for use, doesn't improve query performance on its own, and doesn't guarantee data cleanliness.

mcqs.question: A source system silently adds a new field and renames another. Under schema-on-read, when is this most likely to be discovered?
options: Immediately at write time, since schema-on-read validates every write against a fixed schema
Never, since schema-on-read makes schema changes irrelevant
The lake automatically alerts on any schema change
Only when a downstream read job tries to interpret the data and breaks or produces wrong results
mcqs.explanation: Because schema-on-read defers schema interpretation to query time, a silent upstream schema change typically isn't caught until a reader actually tries to interpret the new shape and fails or misbehaves. Schema-on-write, not schema-on-read, validates at write time, and neither model makes schema changes irrelevant or automatically alerts without added tooling.

mcqs.question: According to the lake-vs-warehouse comparison, which statement correctly reflects the trade-off?
options: A data lake typically wins on storage cost and schema flexibility, while a warehouse typically wins on query performance and governance
A warehouse always wins on every dimension, including storage cost
A data lake always provides stronger ACID guarantees than a warehouse
Query performance is identical between lakes and warehouses out of the box
mcqs.explanation: The comparison shows lakes ahead on cost and flexibility and warehouses ahead on out-of-the-box query performance and governance — neither dominates every dimension. Warehouses don't win on storage cost, lakes historically have weaker ACID guarantees without an added layer, and out-of-the-box query performance clearly favors the warehouse.

mcqs.question: What actually causes a data lake to become a 'data swamp'?
options: Storing too much raw data in object storage, regardless of process
An accumulation of small process gaps — no assigned ownership, no enforced zone convention, no lineage tracking — rather than one single failure
Using schema-on-read instead of schema-on-write
Object storage becoming full
mcqs.explanation: The swamp accumulates from many individually-reasonable shortcuts — skipped documentation, unowned one-off exports, unenforced conventions — not from data volume itself or from schema-on-read as a model. Object storage running out of space is essentially a non-issue given its scalability, and schema-on-read is a design choice, not the direct cause of a swamp.

mcqs.question: Why did plain object-storage-backed lakes historically lack ACID guarantees for table-like updates?
options: Object storage was designed for durable whole-file storage, not fine-grained, multi-file transactional updates that appear atomic to readers
ACID guarantees are impossible for any storage system, including databases
Object storage is too slow to support any kind of write
Lakes never needed ACID guarantees because they don't support concurrent access
mcqs.explanation: Object storage's design for durable file storage, not multi-file atomic updates, is exactly why a table represented as a directory of files had no native way to make a multi-file update appear atomic to readers. Databases achieve ACID guarantees routinely, object storage write speed isn't the limiting factor here, and lakes do support concurrent access, which is precisely what creates the consistency risk described.
